The ending feels completely natural and earned because it completes the narrator's internal character arc and resolves the central tension of the story. Throughout the first visit, the narrator frequently corrects the mother and pushes back against her stubbornness and altered memories—specifically arguing over who was frightened during a childhood trip to the beach. After the mother's health crisis, the narrator realizes that the mother's habits and assertions were simply her way of maintaining control over a shrinking world. When the mother brings up the ocean trip again at the very end, the narrator no longer corrects her ("I might have been"). This shift from resistance to gentle acceptance, paired with the final image of the mother's open hand—contrasting her earlier grasp on the trowel, key, and dish towel—provides a deeply resonant and purposeful sense of closure.
